topics: 🦶 An Odd Sandal — with a foot-wound, does the sandal go on the sore foot or the healthy one?
👟 Right Foot First? — Rabbi Yoḥanan's tefillin-parallel and how to satisfy both customs
📿 Tefillin on Shabbat — forbidden and exempt from a sin-offering, for two independent reasons
🧿 What Proves an Amulet 'From an Expert' — the writer's track record vs. the amulet's own
🔥 Do Amulets Carry Sanctity? — testing it against fire, burial, and the bathroom

overview.title: 📖 Overview: Sandals, Shoe-Laces, Tefillin, and Amulets
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 61a–61b
overview.hebrewSource: וְלֹא בְּקָמֵיעַ בִּזְמַן שֶׁאֵינוֹ מִן הַמּוּמְחֶה
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by finishing the mishna's single-sandal case — when a foot wound justifies wearing only one sandal, which foot gets it? — and widens into the order in which one puts on shoes, ties them, washes, and applies oil, weighing Rabbi Yoḥanan's tefillin-based custom against a conflicting baraita. It then returns to the mishna's list, explaining through Rav Safra why tefillin are forbidden on Shabbat and why going out with them still carries no sin-offering liability, regardless of the dispute over whether Shabbat is even a day for tefillin. The rest of the daf works out exactly what makes an amulet 'from an expert' — testing combinations of writers and amulets — and closes by asking whether amulets carry any sanctity, checking that question against saving them from a fire, burying them when discarded, and entering a bathroom while wearing one.

slides.title: 🦶 An Odd Sandal — Which Foot?
slides.subtitle: With a wound, the mishna permits a single sandal — but on which foot?

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: The mishna implies: with a wound on the foot, one MAY go out wearing a single sandal. On which foot does he wear it?

lines.speaker: Rav Huna
lines.text: On the wounded foot. A sandal exists to prevent pain — wearing just one shows everyone it's for the wound, not for hiding a carried sandal.

lines.speaker: Ḥiyya bar Rav
lines.text: On the healthy foot! A sandal exists for comfort, and the visible wound on the other foot itself explains why it has none.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: Rabbi Yoḥanan told his attendant, 'Give me my sandal.' Handed the RIGHT one, he objected: 'You've made this foot into a wounded one!' Doesn't that prove he follows Rav Huna?

lines.speaker: Rejection
lines.text: Not necessarily — he may have meant the opposite: 'you've made my bare LEFT foot look wounded,' which fits Ḥiyya bar Rav instead.

callout.label: Left unresolved:
callout.text: The exchange with Rabbi Yoḥanan's attendant cannot decide between the two views.

slides.title: 👟 Right Foot First? Reconciling Two Customs
slides.subtitle: Rabbi Yoḥanan's tefillin-parallel meets a conflicting baraita

steps.content: 1️⃣ Rabbi Yoḥanan: 'like tefillin, so shoes' — tefillin go on the LEFT arm, so a shoe goes on the LEFT foot first
2️⃣ Objection, from a baraita: 'One puts on the right shoe, and afterward the left'
3️⃣ Rav Yosef: since both are taught, either practice is valid — 'one who did this way, did properly; one who did that way, did properly'
4️⃣ Abaye pushes back: maybe Rabbi Yoḥanan simply never heard this baraita — a real ruling is still needed
5️⃣ Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak: 'one who fears Heaven fulfills both' — like Mar, son of Rabbana, who puts on the right shoe untied, then the left shoe tied, then goes back and ties the right

callout.label: Also taught:
callout.text: Removing shoes: left off first, then right, so the right stays on longest. Washing and oiling: right first, then left — but oiling the whole body starts at the head, 'king over all the limbs.'

slides.title: 📿 Tefillin on Shabbat — Forbidden and Exempt, Either Way
slides.subtitle: Rav Safra's two independent rulings
slides.label: Rav Safra:
slides.text: The mishna forbids going out with tefillin. Do not say this is only because some hold Shabbat is not a proper day for donning tefillin at all — even for those who hold it IS a proper day, one may not go out wearing them, lest he come to carry them by hand through the public domain. And on the mishna's closing line, that one who does go out incurs no sin-offering: do not say that is only true for those who hold Shabbat IS a day for tefillin (so no violation occurs at all) — even for those who hold it is NOT, he is still exempt, דֶּרֶךְ מַלְבּוּשׁ עֲבִידָא, because wearing tefillin is done in the manner of a garment, not blatant carrying.

slides.title: 🧿 What Proves an Amulet 'From an Expert'
slides.subtitle: Rav Pappa separates two questions: is the WRITER an expert, and is the AMULET itself effective?
rows: 3 amulets, 3 people, each healed 3 times (9 total cures)
3 amulets for 1 person, all healed him

callout.label: Baseline (Tosefta):
callout.text: An amulet counts as 'from an expert' once it has healed one person three times, whether written or made of herbal roots, and whether the patient was dangerously ill or not.

slides.title: 🔥 Do Amulets Carry Sanctity?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests the question against three practical halakhot

nodes.content: ❓ Do amulets bearing Torah verses and Divine names carry sanctity?

columns.label: Rescue from a Shabbat fire?
columns.content: NO — a baraita: blessings and amulets, even with Torah passages, are not saved; they burn in place

columns.label: Require burial (geniza) if discarded?
columns.content: YES — by analogy: God's name on a vessel's handle or a bed-leg must be cut off and buried

nodes.content: 🚻 Third test: may one enter a bathroom wearing one? The mishna implies yes — 'not with an amulet, unless from an expert' — so an expert's amulet may be worn everywhere, bathroom included
✅ Since its power to heal doesn't depend on where it's worn, one may even carry it in his HAND on Shabbat, not only around the neck

summary.principle: Practices around wearing something into the public domain — a lone sandal, a shoe, tefillin, an amulet — are shaped by whether the item looks like ordinary clothing or invites removal and carrying, while an amulet's own status turns on separately proven facts about its writer and about itself.

flowSteps.content: 🦶 A single sandal with a wound: worn wound-side (Rav Huna) or healthy-side (Ḥiyya bar Rav)
📿 Tefillin forbidden out of concern for carrying; exempt from liability since worn 'like a garment'

columns.content: 🧿 An amulet is 'from an expert' once either the writer's or the amulet's own record is proven
🔥 Amulets: not rescued from fire, yet buried like sacred texts when discarded

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: an item worn 'in the manner of a garment' does not carry Torah-level liability, even when the Sages still forbid wearing it out ab initio

quiz.q: According to Rav Huna, why does a person with a wound on one foot wear his single sandal on the WOUNDED foot rather than the healthy one?
o: Because sandals are worn for comfort, not pain relief
Because a sandal is meant to prevent pain, so wearing just one clearly signals the wound rather than a hidden, carried sandal
Because it hides the wound from view
Because the mishna requires it explicitly
quiz.e: Rav Huna holds a sandal is worn to avoid pain; seeing only one on the wounded foot makes clear why, removing any suspicion that the other is being carried.

quiz.q: How does the God-fearing person described by Rav Naḥman bar Yitzḥak satisfy both traditions about which shoe goes on first?
o: He wears sandals on both feet at once
He puts on the right shoe without tying it, then puts on and ties the left shoe, then goes back and ties the right
He alternates the order by day of the week
He avoids wearing shoes with laces entirely
quiz.e: Mar, son of Rabbana, put the right shoe on first (satisfying the baraita) but left it untied, tied the left shoe first (satisfying Rabbi Yoḥanan's tefillin-based custom), then returned to tie the right.

quiz.q: According to Rav Safra, why does the mishna forbid going out with tefillin on Shabbat even according to the view that Shabbat IS an appropriate day to don tefillin?
o: Because tefillin may only ever be worn in a synagogue
Out of concern that one might come to carry them by hand through the public domain
Because tefillin are considered a forbidden mixture
Because Shabbat tefillin must always remain in a case
quiz.e: Rav Safra explains the prohibition applies regardless of that dispute, since the real concern is that the person might remove and carry the tefillin in the public domain.

quiz.q: If a single amulet healed three different people, what does this prove according to Rav Pappa?
o: Both the amulet and its writer are proven
Only the amulet itself is proven effective — the writer is not thereby proven an expert
Only the writer is proven an expert — the amulet is not proven effective
Nothing at all is proven
quiz.e: Rav Pappa held that one amulet healing three different people proves the amulet's own effectiveness, but does not establish that its writer is a general expert.

quiz.q: What did the Gemara conclude about amulets containing Torah verses or Divine names, regarding fire and burial?
o: They must be rescued from a fire on Shabbat and need not be buried
They are not rescued from a fire (they burn in place) but must be buried like sacred texts when discarded
They have no sanctity at all in either regard
They may never be written with Divine names in the first place
quiz.e: A baraita teaches that amulets are not saved from a Shabbat fire, yet by analogy to Divine names on vessel handles or bed legs, they require burial (geniza) once discarded.
